e-8473.knowledge_point: Identifying the Principal Axes of a Quadratic Curve Using a Diagram
e-8473.problem:
Draw a diagram that depicts the lines representing the principal axes of the quadratic curve shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/5354b2fa6d2fb2c8b1b9ea3cb675225619e8debe64e1ec108b556248d6e672ec.png)
e-8473.worked_solution:
The principal axes of a curve define a coordinate system in which the curve can be represented by its (simplest) canonical equation. 

Our curve is a hyperbola. This curve will have the canonical equation of the form

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{a^2} - \dfrac{y^2}{b^2} = 1
$$

if one axis passes through the vertices of the hyperbola and the other axis is the perpendicular bisector of the segment connecting the two vertices.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/bd0d117543012be1c4eab0acda878c9aea67518e46c93048e8c249de1a0c03e6.png)

e-8277.problem: Which curve is defined by the equation $6x_1^2+8x_1x_2-9x_2^2= 70?$
e-8277.worked_solution:
Consider the quadratic form $Q(\mathbf{x})=6x_1^2+8x_1x_2-9x_2^2.$ To  determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce $Q(\mathbf{x})$ to its canonical (diagonal) form.

First, we write down the matrix of $Q(\mathbf{x}),$ which is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14076805/assets/33a30f2c07875359a60caed74f802a2de29ac9e44089800ed8f30a2015303bce.png)

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}6-\lambda  & 4 \\ 4 & -9-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda -70 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =7,\,-10\end{aligned}
$$

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to $7y_1^2 -10 y_2^2.$  

In the new variables, the curve has the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}7{y}_{1}^{2}-10{y}_{2}^{2} & =70 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{10}-\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{7} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{(\sqrt{10})^{2}}-\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{(\sqrt{7})^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This is a hyperbola with semiaxes $\sqrt{10}$ and $\sqrt{7}.$

decision.explanation: The quadratic-form matrix is [[5,1],[1,5]], with eigenvalues 6 and 4. In orthonormal principal coordinates, the equation becomes 6y₁²+4y₂²=12, or y₁²/2+y₂²/3=1. Thus it is an ellipse with semiaxes √2 and √3.
